I may be downvoted to hell for this, but there are benefits to eating organic versions of healthy food (read: *not* organic food, period, but organic versions of already established healthy foods). A lot of the pesticides, herbicides and radiation treatment lots of produce get are often considered potential (*small*, but still potential) cancer risks. Plus, with all the controversy around pesticides and the increasing strength of the pests they're intended to ward off, having produce that doesn't use them is a means of attempting to relieve this. But more important than organic produce is organic animal products. With such huge instances of animal rights abuse in factory farms, where "organic" guarantees at least a certain degree of care and good treatment of the animals, one can see why it may have such wide appeal. Plus, it makes you think differently of the food you're eating when the animal it comes from has differences in the growth hormones its given, and the health of the animal before it's killed. Plus, it's just more ethical for the animals. Look, obviously in the best case scenario we'd all be vegetarians, and regardless of the situation the animals are still killed for our food. But hey, if you're going to eat meat, wouldn't you rather the animal have lived a more pleasant life rather than suffer in a factory farm with terrible conditions? So yeah, it's not completely confirmed that organic food is not in any way, shape or form healthier than conventional food. It also goes way beyond health reasons why people would switch to organic. QUICKEDIT: It is not confirmed that organic food is not healthier. It is, however, unconfirmed how big of the difference is and that's what skeptics go on about. EDIT: OK screw it, my definition for organic farming was very much wrong. Still, there are some differences in the same vein. But you have every right to criticize me for what I have specified as the differences.

Hype isn't the only thing that settles with movies like this--**anti-hype comes around right afterwards** and settles soon after. We a huge hype train, and then in the weeks soon after there was a huge hate train. This is something that you need to understand--**it goes both ways**. For me, I saw it opening night. I absolutely loved it. I then saw it three days later with my relatives. Still absolutely loved it. Most friends of mine saw it around that same opening week. We all still love it. Some of my friends didn't like it as much--that's fine. When the hate train started rolling around on the internet, I admit I started to doubt my opinions on the movie. But then I rewatched episodes 4 and 5 with a friend (his first time seeing them), and rewatching them, I noticed that while people claim the new film is derivative, the feel, and many of its features on a much deeper level, are far different, but they still feel very much like the franchise. Looking back at the new film, I was even more fond of it. After seeing some **people on the internet claim, "the prequels were better than this! At least they were original!"**, I had to go back and watch Episode II (since I do own it) with my sibling out of curiosity. We said before watching, "Maybe the prequels are not actually that bad. Maybe the originals just set a high standard." We were wrong. **And holy shit are those people overreacting**. The new film probably should've been another 2 or 3 minutes longer to get some more exposition, but I vastly preferred that to EpII, which had at least a solid hour's worth of content I just wished I hadn't seen. **Better to keep me wanting more than wanting enormously less.** **Over a month afterwards, and I still love the new film.** Now that the hate train has mostly rolled by and has settled, I'm even more sure of how much I love the movie. Most of my friends who saw it when it opened loved it. Most of my friends who have just seen it recently loved it. It certainly has flaws, and I want Episodes 8 and 9 to be more divergent (which the director claims was the intended effect--that Ep7 would reground and 8 and 9 would take things further), but what I'm most impressed by is that **it was all of the new elements of the film that I loved most** (the new characters, the fact that the villain wasn't a clone of the old villain, humanizing the soldiers, making the soldiers actually capable fighters, the overall main new plot, the new lightsaber choreography, and the general quality of the filmmaking). So yeah. I'll claim that the new film was really that good. I can't rank it against Episodes 4, 5 and 6 yet because the new trilogy is not complete yet and both trilogies rely on their neighboring movies, but I can easily say that I enjoyed it far more than any of the prequels. That is a point I can make even without having seen the rest of this trilogy. Also, here's an awesome video by a film reviewer that really says it better than I can. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YbaliPyihCY. It brings up an excellent parallel situation in the Indiana Jones franchise.

Not only that, but rewatching Episodes I and II, they have just as many nostalgic callbacks, and many come off as super forced and just to be there. The new film was *definitely* not the movie to start doing this.

A few things: 1) Humor is not the same thing as cheese. You seem to be mixing the two. Cheese in movies is actually more like failed melodrama in nature. Or things like puns for comedy. And the exploitation of cheese can be used for clever humor. I'll actually use one of your examples to demonstrate my point: >A character: Wait, why are you helping me? >Another character: ...because it's the right thing to do. If the scene had left off over here, that would have been ridiculously cheesy. That's like the silliest Hollywood trope ever where someone does something good because of some arbitrary sense of what's "right" and "wrong" without any exposure to it. >[small pause] >A character: ...you need a pilot. >Another character:...I need a pilot. This actually diverted potential cheese into clever humor, by subverting a typical trope used, and turning it on its head. Suddenly, the second character isn't just some guy who somehow is asserting these arbitrary morals that he doesn't know--he's a desperate opportunist. 2) Different properties have different thresholds of cheese, and different pieces of dialogue have different levels of it. For example, none of these lines, whether humorous or not, would fit at all in a horror film. But in a space opera film, they fit perfectly fine. The reason why I still got disrupted by the spin-off's cheesiness is because it got so cheesy it actually crossed even the franchise's line. Which I honestly wasn't sure was so possible. 3) Delivery is also key. Every single one of the lines you cited could've been too cheesy and stupid in the wrong actor's hands, or with bad direction. But each of those moments you cited were delivered extremely well, with tone to match. So it worked, and never took me out of the film. But with the spin-off, half of the time there was a cheesy line it was delivered *extremely* poorly, or given bad direction to the inflection was off. Or, just didn't belong tone-wise. It also hurts the movie because it was supposed to be a grittier title, and yet it was even cheesier than the latest installment, so there was some stark and distracting tonal inconsistency.  It reminded me, to a lesser extent of my comparison of a superhero team-up film and a darker superhero film (though to a far lesser extent): the former was able to stay pretty light and still not cross its line of cheesiness, while the latter tried to be far grittier and yet was far cheesier.

If you're doing postgame, here's the best tip: **once you hit low 80s, fight a specific enemy type in a specific region over and over again. Finish him off with a chain attack. Don't approach him from the back or he'll probably one-shot you.** Killing him that way will give you over a full level's exp for each kill. Even after you're higher level than him, they'll still each give you about half a level. It's amazing--I did side quests for 20 hours or so at level 81 (mostly because they get really good in the second half of the game) and gained about 2 levels. I've already beaten a couple, but I really want to take on a few that are ridiculously hard. What's great about this game as an improvement over the first entry is that difference in level doesn't give stupid invisible buffs or debuffs in itself. So these superbosses are actually doable without cheesing the game. In the first game, an enemy 5 or 6 levels higher than you literally debuffs your hit rate by 150%. Never the case in this sequel.
